fields.expected: I submitted jobright-application-agent, a local Playwright-based job-application agent I wrote in TypeScript and Node. The problem was that job hunting is mostly repetitive browser work: finding roles, opening ATS pages, refilling the same information, tracking state. But a fully autonomous browser agent is dangerous here, because one wrong action submits a real application or fabricates an answer in a legal or demographic field. So I built it as a deterministic, operator-controlled agent instead. Every application moves through an explicit state machine (DISCOVERED through ELIGIBILITY_CHECK, FILL, READY_TO_SUBMIT, SUBMITTED, COMPLETED) rather than being mutated ad hoc, and SQLite is the single source of truth because state diverging across processes is what makes automation unsafe. Every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED that never default on. I also built a validation ladder from UNIT_CONFIRMED to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED, so a capability is not called working just because it passes against a fixture. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from auto-fill and always generate a human-review item. It supports Greenhouse, partially Lever and Ashby, and deliberately skips Workday and iCIMS rather than handling them unreliably.

fields.expected: Replit is building the thing I keep running into from the other side. I have shipped products that real people used: ClarityAtlas, an iOS health app I built end to end in Swift, SwiftUI, and Supabase, including a passive sleep-estimation system from HealthKit and Core Motion signals, which went into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users. Most of the difficulty was never the model or the idea, it was the distance between something working on my machine and something a user can actually run. That is the gap Replit closes, and doing it through natural language for millions of people is a much harder version of the problem than the one I solved for myself. The part I would want to work on is the reliability layer. At Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, and it convinced me that generating output is cheap while deciding whether to trust it is hard. Agentic software creation has the same asymmetry: correctness, failure modes, and where the agent should stop and ask a human matter more as generation gets cheaper.
